title: Interface Satisfaction
story: Your chat app now has three message sources: people typing, bots auto-responding, and pet status updates. You want ONE notification function. The beauty of interfaces: all three types satisfy Greetable, so your single function handles them all without a single if-statement.
why: Multiple types satisfying the same interface enables polymorphic code — one function, many behaviors, chosen automatically based on the actual type at runtime.
analogy: Interface satisfaction is like a universal power outlet — any device (type) that has the right plug (methods) can connect. Your lamp, laptop, and phone charger all work in the same outlet because they all satisfy the 'pluggable' interface. The outlet doesn't care what the device does, only that it fits.
try_it: Add a `Dog` type (fields: name, breed) that greets with a bark. Add an `Alien` that greets in a made-up language. Count how many types you can make Greetable. Then try passing an Int to `announce` — what error do you get? The compiler tells you exactly why Int doesn't qualify (it has no `greet` method).
tips: Any type that has the interface methods IS that interface — no declaration needed
The interface only guarantees those methods exist — the function can't access type-specific fields
Multiple types can satisfy the same interface with COMPLETELY different implementations
common_mistakes: Expecting to access type-specific fields inside a generic function — `thing.name` doesn't work; only `thing.greet()` is guaranteed
Trying to put different types in one Vec[Greetable] — interfaces constrain GENERICS, they aren't a common type for collections
Forgetting that each type needs its OWN method definition — `fn Person.greet`, `fn Robot.greet`, etc.
